  3. Jahr or Jahre? Complete Lena's age.
    Ich bin neunzehn alt.
5

Das Alphabet (the alphabet)

Your notes teach what each letter sounds like. This teaches what each letter is called — which is the part you need to spell your name at a German counter.

Die zwei Regeln (the two that carry this Lektion)

Buchstabenname ≠ Buchstabenklang (letter name ≠ letter sound)

Your notes teach the sound (A wie Apfel). This Lektion adds the name — what you say when you spell aloud. Four pairs trip up English speakers, and they are worth drilling as pairs: A=AH vs E=AY, E=AY vs I=EE, G=GAY vs J=YOT, V=FOW vs W=VAY. On the phone, add wie + Wort to any letter that rhymes — B, D, E, P and T all sound alike down a bad line.

Umlaut und Eszett (umlaut and Eszett)

Ä Ö Ü are not separate basic letters — they are A, O, U with two dots — but the dots change the word: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful). If you cannot type them, write ae, oe, ue; never just drop them. ß is called Eszett, always sounds like a sharp hissed s, and can never start a word. For this sharp s sound, a long vowel or diphthong before it usually takes ß (Fuß, Straße); a short vowel takes ss (Fluss, Kuss).

Buchstabe (the letters)

  • 🔤der Buchstabe / die Buchstabenletter (of the alphabet)
  • 🍎A aAH · “der Apfel / die Äpfel” — apple · English says “ay” — German says AH.
  • 🍌B bBAY · “die Banane / die Bananen” — banana · rhymes with D, E, P, T — use “B wie Banane” on the phone.
  • 🛋️C cTSAY · “die Couch / die Couches” — couch · not “see”. C alone is rare in German; it usually appears in ch and sch.
  • 🇩🇪D dDAY · “Deutschland” — Germany · rhymes with B, E, P, T.
  • 🐘E eAY · “der Elefant / die Elefanten” — elephant · English “ee” is German I. The whole vowel row is shifted.
  • 🐟F fEFF · “der Fisch / die Fische” — fish · the letter name is essentially the same as in English.
  • 🎸G gGAY · “die Gitarre / die Gitarren” — guitar · the letter name begins with a hard g.
  • 🏠H hHAH · “das Haus / die Häuser” — house · not “aitch”. A silent lengthening h can follow a vowel, as in Uhr.
  • 🦔I iEE · “der Igel / die Igel” — hedgehog · English “eye” is German EI. German I is a plain EE.
  • 🥣J jYOT · “der Joghurt / die Joghurts” — yoghurt · German J usually sounds like English Y, while its letter name is YOT.
  • ☕K kKAH · “der Kaffee / die Kaffees” — coffee · unlike English “kay”, German K is KAH.
  • ❤️L lELL · “die Liebe” — love (no usual plural) · the letter name is essentially the same as in English.
  • 👨M mEMM · “der Mann / die Männer” — man · the letter name is essentially the same as in English.
  • 🔩N nENN · “der Nagel / die Nägel” — nail · double n is said Doppel-N when spelling aloud.
  • 🍊O oOH · “die Orange / die Orangen” — orange · close to English O, but without its final w-glide.
  • 🐧P pPAY · “der Pinguin / die Pinguine” — penguin · not “pee”. Rhymes with B, D, E, T.
  • ❓Q qKOO · “das Quiz / die Quiz” — quiz · not “kyoo”. In native German words, q is followed by u.
  • 🔴R rERR · “Rot” — red · a throat r, similar to Urdu غ, is common in Standard German; after a vowel it may weaken toward -uh.
  • ☀️S sESS · “die Sonne / die Sonnen” — sun · at the start of a word before a vowel, s usually buzzes like English z: Sonne = ZON-uh.
  • 🍵T tTAY · “der Tee / die Tees” — tea · not “tee” as in golf — it rhymes with B, D, E, P.
  • ⏰U uOO · “die Uhr / die Uhren” — clock · not “yoo”. A plain oo.
  • 🐦V vFOW · “der Vogel / die Vögel” — bird · the name rhymes with English how. In native words such as Vogel, v is usually pronounced f; some loanwords use a v sound.
  • ☁️W wVAY · “die Wolke / die Wolken” — cloud · not “double-u”. German w normally has the English v sound: Wolke = VOL-kuh.
  • 🎶X xIKS · “das Xylofon / die Xylofone” — xylophone · rare in German. Same sound as English x.
  • 🐃Y yEWP-si-lon · “der Yak / die Yaks” — yak · a whole three-syllable word, not one letter-sound.
  • 🦓Z zTSETT · “das Zebra / die Zebras” — zebra · not “zed”, not “zee”. In native German words, z has the ts sound.
  • 🐻Ä äEH · “der Bär / die Bären” — bear · say the sound itself. It is A with an Umlaut — not a separate basic letter.
  • 🛢️Ö öOE · “das Öl / die Öle” — oil · say the sound itself: “ay” with rounded lips, no r in it.
  • 5️⃣Ü üEW · “fünf” — five · say the sound itself: “ee” with tightly rounded lips.
  • 🦶ßess-TSETT · “der Fuß / die Füße” — foot · called Eszett or scharfes S. Always a sharp hissed s, and it can never start a word.

Buchstabieren (spelling aloud)

  • ❓Wie schreibt man das?vee SHR-EYE-pt man das · How do you write that? · the everyday way to ask for a spelling.
  • 🔤Buchstabieren Sie, bitte!BOOKH-shtah-BEE-rn zee, BIT-uh · /ˌbuːxʃtaˈbiːʁən ziː ˈbɪtə/ · formell (formal) Please spell it! · another Sie-command — verb first, Sie second, bitte to soften. Same shape as Wiederholen Sie!
  • 🍎A wie ApfelAH vee AP-fl · A as in Apfel · the repair move that saves you on the phone, because B, D, E, P and T all rhyme.
  • 🔠großes A / kleines aGROH-sess AH / KL-EYE-ness AH · capital A / small a · needed whenever a name starts with a capital or contains one. groß itself contains a ß.
  • 🔁Doppel-NDOP-l ENN · double N · Schmitt = S – C – H – M – I – Doppel-T.

Regel (rule)

  • ✏️Ä Ö Ü sind keine neuen BuchstabenUmlauts are A, O, U with two dots — not separate basic letters · the dots change the word: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful). Cannot type them? Write ae, oe, ue.
  • ⚖️ß oder ss?For the sharp s sound: long vowel or diphthong → ß · short vowel → ss · Fuß, Straße, weiß (long) — Fluss, Kuss, muss (short). Switzerland always writes ss.
  • ⚠️Die vier FallenA/E, E/I, G/J, V/W · German A=AH, E=AY, I=EE — shifted from English. J=YOT, V=FOW, W=VAY. Drill them as pairs.

Dialog 1 — Im Hotel (at the hotel)

🛎️ Rezeption
Guten Abend! Wie ist Ihr Familienname?Good evening! What is your surname?
🙋 Gast
Ahmad.Ahmad.
🛎️ Rezeption
Wie schreibt man das?How do you write that?
🙋 Gast
A – H – M – A – D.A-H-M-A-D.
🛎️ Rezeption
Noch einmal, bitte! Langsam.Once again, please! Slowly.
🙋 Gast
A wie Apfel – H wie Haus – M wie Mann – A – D wie Deutschland.A as in Apfel, H as in Haus, M as in Mann, A, D as in Deutschland.
🛎️ Rezeption
Danke schön! Zimmer vierundzwanzig.Thank you kindly! Room twenty-four.
🙋 Gast
Vielen Dank!Thank you very much!

📌 The first attempt fails, so the guest switches to wie + Wort. That is the normal repair move, not bad German. The room number is vierundzwanzig — unit first, straight from Lektion 4.

Dialog 2 — Der Umlaut (the umlaut)

🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Wie heißen Sie mit Familiennamen?What is your surname?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Öztürk
Öztürk.Öztürk.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Buchstabieren Sie, bitte!Please spell it!
🙋‍♂️ Herr Öztürk
Großes Ö – Z – T – Ü – R – K.Capital Ö – Z – T – Ü – R – K.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Ö wie Öl?Ö as in Öl?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Öztürk
Ja, genau. Ö wie Öl.Yes, exactly. Ö as in Öl.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Danke!Thanks!

📌 großes Ö tells her it is a capital. genau (exactly) is a bonus word Germans use constantly — recognise it. Wie heißen Sie …? belongs to Lektion 7; recognise-only here.

Dialog 3 — V oder W? (on the telephone)

☎️ Frau Ott
Wie ist Ihr Name?What is your name?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Weber
Weber.Weber.
☎️ Frau Ott
Mit V oder mit W?With V or with W?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Weber
Mit W — W wie Wolke.With W — W as in Wolke.
☎️ Frau Ott
Ah! W – E – B – E – R.Ah! W-E-B-E-R.
🙋‍♂️ Herr Weber
Genau. Danke!Exactly. Thanks!
☎️ Frau Ott
Bitte. Auf Wiederhören!You're welcome. Goodbye!

📌 This is THE German phone question, because V (FOW) and W (VAY) are the pair English speakers mix up most. Auf Wiederhören, not Auf Wiedersehen, because it is a phone call.

Dialog 4 — Straße oder Strasse? (ß or ss?)

👨‍🏫 Lehrer
Wie schreibt man „Fuß“?How do you write “Fuß”?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
F – U – Eszett.F – U – Eszett.
👨‍🏫 Lehrer
Sehr gut! Und „Fluss“?Very good! And “Fluss”?
🙋‍♀️ Sara
F – L – U – Doppel-S.F – L – U – double S.
👨‍🏫 Lehrer
Genau! Fuß mit Eszett, Fluss mit Doppel-S.Exactly! Fuß with ß, Fluss with ss.
🙋‍♀️ Sara
Danke!Thanks!

📌 The long u in Fuß takes ß; the short u in Fluss takes ss. That is the whole rule. sehr gut is recognise-only — it comes back properly in Lektion 8.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau beim Buchstabieren (sentence structure for spelling)

1 · Wie schreibt man das? (How do you write that?) — a W-question with man
WieW-Wort · question wordschreibtVerb · position 2manSubjekt · one, youdas?Objekt · that

man is the general "one / you / people", so Wie schreibt man das? is literally "How does one write that?" — the everyday request for a spelling, used to open Dialog 1. The W-word takes position 1, the verb stays glued to position 2, and the subject follows.

2 · Buchstabieren Sie, bitte! (Please spell it!) — the formal imperative
BuchstabierenVerb · position 1SieSubjekt · formal youbitte!softener

A polite instruction to a stranger puts the verb first and Sie right after it, exactly like Wiederholen Sie! (Lektion 8). Adding bitte turns a command into a request — the shape the Beamtin uses in Dialog 2.

3 · Wie ist Ihr Familienname? (What is your surname?) — sein (to be) + formal possessive
WieW-Wort · question wordistVerb · position 2Ihr Familienname?Subjekt · formal possessive

The receptionist's opener from Dialog 1: W-word, then sein in position 2, then the subject. Ihr capitalised is the formal possessive (Lektion 24) — lowercase ihr would mean "her/their". Wie heißen Sie? (Dialog 2) asks the same thing a different way and belongs properly to Lektion 7.

4 · Buchstabe (letter) + wie (as in) + Beispielwort (example word) — the repair formula
ABuchstabe · letterwieas, likeApfelBeispielwort · example word

Not a full sentence but a fixed three-piece chunk, repeated for every letter that might be misheard: A wie Apfel, H wie Haus, M wie Mann, D wie Deutschland (Dialog 1), Ö wie Öl (Dialog 2), W wie Wolke (Dialog 3). It exists because B, D, E, P, T all rhyme down a bad phone line.

5 · Mit V oder mit W? (With V or W?) — the confusable-letter check
Mit Vmit · with + Buchstabe · letteroderormit W?mit · with + Buchstabe · letter

A short fragment, not a full clause — mit (with) plus the bare letter, used specifically for the one pair German speakers themselves cannot always tell apart by ear: V (FOW) and W (VAY). Frau Ott asks this after hearing Herr Weber's surname.

6 · Scharfes s: lang → ß, kurz → ss (sharp s: long → ß, short → ss) — a spelling rule, not a verb form
Fußlanger Vokal · long vowel → ßFlusskurzer Vokal · short vowel → ss

No subject or verb here — this chip pair shows the spelling of the sharp s sound from Dialog 4: the long u in Fuß is followed by ß; the short u in Fluss is followed by ss. This contrast applies when the consonant is a sharp, voiceless s sound.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • A-E-I slide one step: German A = ah, E = ay, I = ee. English A resembles German E, and English E resembles German I; learn German A separately as AH.
  • J is Y: Joghurt is "yoghurt". Since J already does Y's job in German, the letter needed its own name: YOT.
  • V and W follow their usual native-word sounds: V is called FOW (rhymes with English how) and is usually f in native words such as Vogel. W is called VAY and normally has the English v sound, as in Wolke (VOL-kuh).
  • Z wie Zebra (Z as in Zebra): a German zebra is a "TSebra". In native German words, Z normally has a ts sound — its letter name is TSETT, not "zed" or "zee".
  • Es-Zett (the names of S + Z): the name Eszett combines Es and Zett. Historically, ß developed from ligatures involving a long s with s or z. It is also called scharfes S (sharp S): hissing like the s of hiss, never buzzing like the s of rose.
  • For sharp s: long → ß, short → ss: after a long vowel or diphthong, write ß (Fuß); after a short vowel, write ss (Fluss).
  • groß (large) has a ß in it: the spelling term großes A means "capital A", and groß itself contains an Eszett.
  • ae, oe, ue instead of nothing: no German keyboard? In ordinary text, write Baer, schoen, fuer rather than dropping the dots. Preserve the official spelling of a person's name whenever possible.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • E said as "ee" → AY — German E = ay. English "ee" is the German letter I.
  • I said as "eye" → EE — German I = ee. English "eye" is the German diphthong ei.
  • J said as "jay" → YOT — German J sounds like English Y.
  • W said as "double-u" → VAY — German W says v, and its name follows the sound.
  • V said as "vee" → FOW — the letter name begins with f and rhymes with how; v is also usually pronounced f in native German words.
  • Z said as "zed" → TSETT — in native German words, Z normally has the ts sound.
  • Bar for Bär → Bär — dropping the umlaut changes the word — or destroys it.
  • fur for für → für (or fuer) — if you cannot type ü, write ue — never nothing.
  • ß at the start of a word → impossible — ß never begins a German word.
  • Fluß → Fluss — for the sharp s sound, a short vowel takes ss; a long vowel or diphthong takes ß.

Dialog An der Rezeption (At the reception desk)

  • RezeptionGuten Tag! Wie ist Ihr Familienname?Hello! What is your surname?
  • BilalFarooq.Farooq.
  • RezeptionWie schreibt man das?How do you write that?
  • BilalF – A – R – Doppel-O – Q.F – A – R – double O – Q.
  • RezeptionMit K oder mit Q?With K or with Q?
  • BilalMit Q. Q wie Quiz.With Q. Q as in Quiz.
  • RezeptionDanke schön! Zimmer sechsunddreißig.Thank you kindly! Room thirty-six.
  • BilalSechsunddreißig? Drei – sechs?Thirty-six? Three – six?
  • RezeptionJa, genau.Yes, exactly.
  • BilalVielen Dank!Thank you very much!

Richtig oder falsch? (true or false?)

  1. Der Familienname ist Farooq. The surname is Farooq.
  2. Man schreibt Farooq mit K. Farooq is written with a K.
  3. Die Zimmernummer ist sechsunddreißig. The room number is thirty-six.

Schreib das fehlende Wort (type it — capital letters count)

  1. Complete the question asking how something is spelled.
    Wie man das?
  2. Complete the repair formula with the lesson's example word for Q.
    Q wie .
  3. Complete the spelling: the two O's are said as one word.
    F – A – R – – Q.
6

Sich vorstellen (Introducing yourself)

The first Lektion where you build sentences instead of learning them whole. Seven pieces of information, one verb pattern, and you can talk about yourself for forty seconds.

Die zwei Regeln (the two rules that carry this Lektion)

1 · Die ich-Form: -en weg, -e dran (the "I"-form: drop -en, add -e)

Take the dictionary form, chop off -en, add -e: wohnen → ich wohne, kommen → ich komme, sprechen → ich spreche. Three very common verbs need special attention: sein → bin, haben → habe, können → kann. Sein and können change their stems here; haben → habe happens to fit the shortcut, although haben is irregular in other forms. High-frequency verbs are often irregular (compare English am, have, can).

2 · Kein Artikel beim Beruf (no article with a job)

English says “I am a student”. In a neutral self-introduction, German says Ich bin Student — no article. After sein, a plain, unmodified job, nationality or religion normally drops the article because German is naming a category, not a thing. Urdu already does this: میں استاد ہوں, with no ایک. Add -in if you are a woman: Lehrerin, Schülerin, Studentin.

Wortschatz: Name & Herkunft (vocabulary: name & where you're from)

Name (name)

All vocabulary expressions in this lesson use a neutral register.

  • 👋Ich heiße …My name is … ikh H-EYE-ssuh · — the everyday one, make this automatic: chop -en off heißen, add -e.
  • 🙋Ich bin …I am … ikh bin · — casual and very common; sein is irregular: bin, not *seine.
  • 🪪Mein Name ist …My name is … m-EYE-n NAH-muh ist · — a touch more formal; der Name → mein, with no -e.
  • 📇Mein Familienname ist …My surname is … m-EYE-n fah-MEE-lee-n-nah-muh ist · — what counters and forms ask for; be ready to spell it (Lektion 5).

Herkunft (origin)

  • 🌍Ich komme aus Pakistan.I come from Pakistan. ikh KOM-uh ows · — aus = out of → your country. You come OUT OF a country.
  • 🏠Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas.I live in Mirpurkhas. ikh VOH-nuh in · — in → your town. You sit IN a town. Never mix aus and in.

Wortschatz: Sprachen & Beruf (vocabulary: languages & job)

Sprachen (languages)

  • 🗣️Ich spreche Deutsch und Englisch.I speak German and English. ikh SHPREKH-uh DOYTCH unt ENG-lish · — Deutsch, NOT Deutsche — Deutsche means German people.
  • 🧠Ich kann Deutsch.I know German. ikh kan DOYTCH · — können normally needs a second verb, but with a language it stands alone.

Beruf (job)

  • 🎓Ich bin Student / Studentin.I am a student (university). ikh bin shtoo-DENT / shtoo-DEN-tin · — no ein in this neutral pattern: plain job titles normally appear without an article after sein, exactly like Urdu: میں استاد ہوں.
  • 🎒Ich bin Schüler / Schülerin.I am a school pupil. ikh bin SHEW-luh / SHEW-luh-rin · — Schüler = school, Student = university. English uses "student" for both — a real trap.
  • 🧑‍🏫Ich bin Lehrer / Lehrerin.I am a teacher. ikh bin LAY-ruh / LAY-luh-rin · — add -in if you are a woman; a woman saying Ich bin Lehrer sounds wrong.

Wortschatz: Familie & Hobby (vocabulary: family & hobby)

Familie (family)

  • 🧍Ich bin ledig.I am single. ikh bin LAY-dikh · — an adjective, so it is negated with nicht, never kein.
  • 💍Ich bin verheiratet.I am married. ikh bin feh-uh-H-EYE-rah-tet · — Ich bin NICHT verheiratet for the negative; an adjective takes nicht.
  • 👶Ich habe ein Kind.I have one child. ikh HAH-buh EYE-n KINT · — haben is irregular. Kind keeps its article here — that rule only drops it for jobs.
  • 🚫Ich habe keine Kinder.I have no children. ikh HAH-buh K-EYE-nuh KIN-duh · — Kinder is a noun → keine, never nicht. Lektion 2's rule doing real work.

Hobby (hobby)

  • 🎨Meine Hobbys sind Elektronik und Bücherlesen.My hobbies are electronics and reading books. M-EYE-nuh HOB-eez zint eh-lek-TROH-nik unt BOO-kher-lay-zn · /ˈmaɪ̯nə ˈhɔbis zɪnt elɛkˈtʁoːnɪk ʊnt ˈbyːçɐˌleːzn̩/ — Bücherlesen combines Bücher (books) + the nominalized verb lesen; nominalized verbs always take a capital, same as Fernsehen elsewhere in this lesson.

Die Regeln kompakt (the rules, as compact recap cards)

  • ✂️Die ich-Formchop -en, add -e — wohnen → ich wohne, kommen → ich komme, sprechen → ich spreche. The first real verb rule.
  • 🚩Die drei Rebellensein → bin · haben → habe · können → kann — memorize these three common verbs: sein and können change their stems here; haben is irregular overall, although ich habe fits the shortcut.
  • 🙅Kein Artikel beim BerufIch bin Student — no ein — after sein, a plain job / nationality / religion normally drops the article. Urdu already does this.
  • 🔗mein · kein · ein bewegen sich zusammen-e before a die-word or a plural — mein Name / meine Hobbys · kein Problem / keine Kinder · ein Mann / eine Frau. One shape, three words.

Nomen aus dieser Lektion (nouns from this lesson — look at the article, not just the word)

  • 🪪der Name / die Namenname
  • 📇der Familienname / die Familiennamensurname
  • 🎓der Student / die Studentenstudent (university) · Studentin for a woman
  • 🎒der Schüler / die Schülerschool pupil · Schülerin for a woman
  • 🧑‍🏫der Lehrer / die Lehrerteacher · Lehrerin for a woman
  • 👶das Kind / die Kinderchild
  • 🎨das Hobby / die Hobbyshobby

In a neutral self-introduction, a plain job noun normally drops its article after sein: Ich bin Student, rather than “Ich bin ein Student” in this pattern. The articles above are the nouns' dictionary forms.

Vier Dialoge: Sich vorstellen (four dialogues: introducing yourself)

Dialog 1 — Im Deutschkurs (in the German class)
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Guten Morgen! Wie heißen Sie?Good morning! What is your name?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich heiße Priyanka. Mein Familienname ist Lohana.My name is Priyanka. My surname is Lohana.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Wie schreibt man das?How do you write that?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
L – O – H – A – N – A.L-O-H-A-N-A.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Danke! Und woher kommen Sie?Thanks! And where do you come from?
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich komme aus Pakistan. Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas.I come from Pakistan. I live in Mirpurkhas.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Sehr gut!Very good!

The spelling comes straight from Lektion 5, and aus (country) sits next to in (town) so you can hear the difference. The questions belong to Lektion 7 — recognise them, answer them.

Dialog 2 — Beruf und Alter (job and age)
🧑‍💼 Herr Weber
Und Sie? Was machen Sie?And you? What do you do?
🙋‍♂️ Bilal
Ich bin Schüler. Ich bin sechzehn Jahre alt.I am a school pupil. I am sixteen years old.
🧑‍💼 Herr Weber
Schüler oder Student?School pupil or university student?
🙋‍♂️ Bilal
Schüler. Ich gehe noch zur Schule.Pupil. I still go to school.
🧑‍💼 Herr Weber
Ah, verstehe!Ah, I see!

Ich bin Schüler, with no ein. And the Schüler/Student distinction is real: he is at school, so Schüler. Ich gehe noch zur Schule is recognise-only.

Dialog 3 — Familie (family)
👩‍💼 Frau Ott
Sind Sie verheiratet?Are you married?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Khan
Nein, ich bin nicht verheiratet. Ich bin ledig.No, I am not married. I am single.
👩‍💼 Frau Ott
Haben Sie Kinder?Do you have children?
🙋‍♂️ Herr Khan
Nein, ich habe keine Kinder.No, I have no children.
👩‍💼 Frau Ott
Danke schön!Thank you kindly!
🙋‍♂️ Herr Khan
Bitte!You're welcome!

The clearest example in the whole course of Lektion 2's rule: nicht verheiratet (an adjective) but keine Kinder (a noun).

Dialog 4 — Sich vorstellen (the full introduction)
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Guten Tag! Ich heiße Priyanka Lohana.Hello! My name is Priyanka Lohana.
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich bin sechzehn Jahre alt.I am sixteen years old.
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich komme aus Pakistan und wohne in Mirpurkhas.I come from Pakistan and live in Mirpurkhas.
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich spreche Deutsch und Englisch.I speak German and English.
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Ich bin Schülerin.I am a school pupil.
🙋‍♀️ Priyanka
Meine Hobbys sind Fernsehen und Musikhören. Danke!My hobbies are watching TV and listening to music. Thank you!
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Sehr gut, Priyanka!Very good, Priyanka!

This is the whole Teil-1 exam answer: seven points, seven short sentences, about forty seconds. Note und wohne — the second ich is dropped because it is the same person, which makes you sound fluent. And Schülerin with -in.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Subjekt + Verb (-en weg, -e dran) + Ergänzung (subject + verb: drop -en, add -e + complement)
IchSubjekt · subjectwohneVerb · position 2in Mirpurkhas.Ort · place

Take the dictionary form, drop -en, add -e: wohnen → ich wohne. In a basic declarative main clause, the conjugated verb sits in position 2. sein → bin and können → kann change their stems; haben → habe fits this shortcut in the ich-form, although the verb is irregular elsewhere.

2 · sein + Beruf — kein Artikel (sein + job — no article)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinVerb · sein (to be)Student.Beruf · job; kein Artikel · no article

After sein, a plain, unmodified job, nationality or religion normally drops the article — German is naming a category, not counting a thing. The neutral self-introduction is Ich bin Student. Urdu already works this way: میں استاد ہوں, with no ایک.

3 · aus vs. in — Herkunft (aus vs. in — origin)
IchSubjekt · subjectkommeVerb · verbaus Pakistan.Land · country of origin
IchSubjekt · subjectwohneVerb · verbin Mirpurkhas.Stadt · town

aus = from/out of → use it for your country of origin. in = in → use it for the town where you live. For the intended meaning “I come from Pakistan,” Ich komme in Pakistan is wrong.

4 · nicht für Adjektive, kein für Nomen (nicht for adjectives, kein for nouns)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinVerb · verbnicht verheiratet.Adjektiv · adjective + nicht
IchSubjekt · subjecthabeVerb · verbkeine Kinder.Nomen · noun + kein

verheiratet is an adjective, so it takes nicht. Kinder is a noun, so it takes kein (here keine, plural) — Lektion 2's rule doing real work in a real sentence.

5 · mein · kein · ein bewegen sich zusammen (mein, kein and ein change together)
mein Namemaskulin · masculine; keine Endung · no endingmeine HobbysPlural · plural; +e

In the nominative forms used here, all three words follow the same pattern: no ending with a masculine or neuter noun, and -e with a feminine noun or a plural. Compare mein Name (masculine, no ending) and meine Hobbys (plural, -e). Other cases can add different endings.

6 · W-Frage: W-Wort + Verb + Subjekt (W-question: question word + verb + subject)
WieW-Wort · question wordheißenVerb · position 2Sie?Subjekt · subject; formal you

A question word takes position 1, the verb stays in position 2, and the subject follows: Wie heißen Sie? Woher kommen Sie? These are the two useful questions in Dialog 1; question patterns are covered in Lektion 7.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • -en weg, -e dran / bin, habe, kann sind die Rebellen (drop -en, add -e / bin, habe and kann are the rebels): Chop -en off the dictionary form and add -e — wohnen → wohne. Memorize sein → bin, haben → habe, können → kann: sein and können change their stems here, while haben → habe fits the shortcut despite being irregular elsewhere.
  • aus dem Land, in der Stadt (from the country, in the town): You come OUT OF a country and sit IN a town. Picture stepping out of Pakistan and sitting down in Mirpurkhas: Ich komme aus Pakistan, ich wohne in Mirpurkhas.
  • Kein „ein“ beim Beruf (no “ein” with a job): In a neutral self-introduction, a plain job title normally has no article after sein. Urdu already gets this right — میں استاد ہوں, no ایک.
  • -in für sie (-in for women): Three letters, always the same: Lehrerin, Schülerin, Studentin.
  • Schule → Schüler, Uni → Student (school → pupil, university → student): The word tells you the building. At Schule you are a Schüler; only at university are you a Student — English blurs both into one word, “student”.
  • mein / kein / ein bewegen sich zusammen (mein / kein / ein change together): In the nominative examples here, all three take -e before a feminine noun or a plural: meine Hobbys, keine Kinder, eine Frau. Learn the shape once.
  • nicht für Adjektive, kein für Nomen (nicht for adjectives, kein for nouns): nicht verheiratet (adjective), keine Kinder (noun) — Lektion 2's rule, still true here.
  • Deutsch ohne -e / Sieben Punkte, vierzig Sekunden (Deutsch without -e / seven points, forty seconds): Here Deutsch names the language; Deutsche can refer to a German person or German people. The self-introduction has seven points — Name, Alter, Land, Wohnort, Sprachen, Beruf, Hobby (name, age, country, town, languages, job, hobby) — and takes about forty seconds.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Ich bin ein Student. → Ich bin Student. — In a neutral self-introduction, plain jobs and nationalities normally drop the article after sein.
  • Ich spreche Deutsche. → Ich spreche Deutsch. — Deutsch = the language. Deutsche = German people.
  • Ich komme in Pakistan. → Ich komme aus Pakistan. — you come OUT OF a country.
  • Ich wohne aus Berlin. → Ich wohne in Berlin. — You live IN a town.
  • (a woman) Ich bin Lehrer. → Ich bin Lehrerin. — Use the -in form that matches you.
  • Ich habe nicht Kinder. → Ich habe keine Kinder. — Kinder is a noun → kein.
  • Ich bin kein verheiratet. → Ich bin nicht verheiratet. — verheiratet is an adjective → nicht.
  • Meine Name ist … → Mein Name ist … — der Name → mein, with no -e.
  • Mein Hobbys sind … → Meine Hobbys sind … — Plural → meine.
  • (at school) Ich bin Student. → Ich bin Schüler. — Schüler = school, Student = university.

Dialog Im Deutschkurs (In the German class)

  • Frau BergerGuten Morgen! Wie heißen Sie?Good morning! What is your name?
  • AyeshaIch heiße Ayesha Khan.My name is Ayesha Khan.
  • Frau BergerWoher kommen Sie, Frau Khan?Where do you come from, Ms Khan?
  • AyeshaIch komme aus Pakistan und wohne in Lahore.I come from Pakistan and live in Lahore.
  • Frau BergerWas machen Sie?What do you do?
  • AyeshaIch bin Studentin. Ich bin zweiundzwanzig Jahre alt.I am a student. I am twenty-two years old.
  • Frau BergerSind Sie verheiratet?Are you married?
  • AyeshaNein, ich bin ledig. Ich habe keine Kinder.No, I am single. I have no children.
  • Frau BergerUnd Ihre Hobbys?And your hobbies?
  • AyeshaMeine Hobbys sind Musikhören und Fernsehen.My hobbies are listening to music and watching TV.

Richtig oder falsch? (true or false?)

  1. Ayesha kommt aus Pakistan. Ayesha comes from Pakistan.
  2. Ayesha ist Lehrerin. Ayesha is a teacher.
  3. Ayesha ist verheiratet. Ayesha is married.

Schreib das fehlende Wort (type it — capital letters count)

  1. Complete with the ich-form of kommen.
    Ich aus Pakistan.
  2. Complete the negation with the right form of kein (Kinder is plural).
    Ich habe Kinder.
  3. Complete Ayesha's sentence about her own hobbies (possessive, plural).
    Hobbys sind Musikhören und Fernsehen.
7

Jemanden kennenlernen (getting to know someone)

Lektion 6 taught you to answer. This one teaches you to ask — and asking is where German grammar finally shows its shape.

Die zwei Regeln (the two that carry this Lektion)

1 · -en für Sie, -st für du (-en for Sie, -st for du)

Most verbs with Sie take the dictionary form unchanged — Sie kommen, Sie wohnen, Sie heißen — which is why the polite form is usually the easy one; sein is the exception: Sie sind. du usually takes -st: du kommst, du wohnst. Two verbs bend: sprechen → du sprichst (e becomes i), and heißen → du heißt (the stem already ends in ß, so only -t is added). Other irregular du forms here are bist / hast / kannst; the matching Sie forms are sind / haben / können.

2 · Wo steht das Verb? (where does the verb stand?)

A W-question puts the question word in slot 1 and the verb in slot 2: Wo wohnen Sie? A yes/no question puts the verb first: Sind Sie verheiratet? There is no do or does — reaching for one means you are speaking English with German words. And the best trick in the Lektion: the question hands you the verb. Take it, put -e on it, and you have your answer.

Sie-Fragen (formal questions · Sie)

  • 📛Wie heißen Sie?What is your name? (Sie) vee H-EYE-ssn zee · — du heißt, not heißst: the stem already ends in ß, so only -t is added.
  • 🪪Wie ist Ihr Familienname?What is your surname? (Sie) vee ist EE-uh fah-MEE-lee-n-nah-muh · — Ihr always takes a capital. Small ihr means her or their.
  • 🌍Woher kommen Sie?Where do you come from? (Sie) vo-HEH-uh KOM-n zee · — woher = where FROM. wo = where, wohin = where to.
  • 🏠Wo wohnen Sie?Where do you live? (Sie) voh VOH-nn zee · — living happens IN a place, so it is wo, never woher.
  • 🎂Wie alt sind Sie?How old are you? (Sie) vee alt zint zee · — sein is the wild one: bin, bist, sind share almost no letters.
  • 🗣️Welche Sprachen sprechen Sie?Which languages do you speak? (Sie) VEL-khuh SHPRAH-khn SHPREKH-n zee · — sprichst, not sprechst: sprechen changes e → i in the du form.
  • 💼Was machen Sie beruflich?What do you do for a living? (Sie) vas MAKH-n zee buh-ROOF-likh · — answer with Ich bin + job, and no article.
  • 🎨Was sind Ihre Hobbys?What are your hobbies? (Sie) vas zint EE-ruh HOB-eez · — plural → Ihre / deine with -e, exactly like meine and keine.
  • 💍Sind Sie verheiratet?Are you married? (Sie) zint zee feh-uh-H-EYE-rah-tet · — a yes/no question: the verb goes FIRST. verheiratet stays lowercase, it is an adjective.
  • 👶Haben Sie Kinder?Do you have children? (Sie) HAH-bn zee KIN-duh · — verb first again. No do/does helper exists in German.

du-Fragen (informal questions · du)

  • 📛Wie heißt du?What is your name? (du) vee H-EYE-sst doo · — du heißt, not heißst: the stem already ends in ß, so only -t is added.
  • 🪪Wie ist dein Familienname?What is your surname? (du) vee ist d-EYE-n fah-MEE-lee-n-nah-muh · — Ihr always takes a capital. Small ihr means her or their.
  • 🌍Woher kommst du?Where do you come from? (du) vo-HEH-uh komst doo · — woher = where FROM. wo = where, wohin = where to.
  • 🏠Wo wohnst du?Where do you live? (du) voh VOHNST doo · — living happens IN a place, so it is wo, never woher.
  • 🎂Wie alt bist du?How old are you? (du) vee alt bist doo · — sein is the wild one: bin, bist, sind share almost no letters.
  • 🗣️Welche Sprachen sprichst du?Which languages do you speak? (du) VEL-khuh SHPRAH-khn SHPRIKHST doo · — sprichst, not sprechst: sprechen changes e → i in the du form.
  • 💼Was machst du beruflich?What do you do for a living? (du) vas makhst doo buh-ROOF-likh · — answer with Ich bin + job, and no article.
  • 🎨Was sind deine Hobbys?What are your hobbies? (du) vas zint D-EYE-nuh HOB-eez · — plural → Ihre / deine with -e, exactly like meine and keine.
  • 💍Bist du verheiratet?Are you married? (du) bist doo feh-uh-H-EYE-rah-tet · — a yes/no question: the verb goes FIRST. verheiratet stays lowercase, it is an adjective.
  • 👶Hast du Kinder?Do you have children? (du) hast doo KIN-duh · — verb first again. No do/does helper exists in German.
Sie- und du-Formen (Sie and du forms of six key verbs)
Verb (verb)Sie (formal you · usually -en)du (informal you · usually -st)
kommen (to come)kommenkommst
wohnen (to live)wohnenwohnst
heißen (to be called)heißenheißt (not heißst)
sprechen (to speak)sprechensprichst (e→i)
sein (to be)sindbist
haben (to have)habenhast

Regeln in Kürze (the rules, in short)

  • 🔤Sie = -en, du = -stthe usual two endings that distinguish the questions — regular verbs use the dictionary form with Sie; remember the exception sein → Sie sind.
  • 🔄du sprichstsprechen changes e → i for du only — also essen → du isst, sehen → du siehst, geben → du gibst. No rule predicts them, learn one at a time.
  • ➡️Verb nach vorn = Ja/Neinmove the verb to the front to ask yes/no — Sie sind verheiratet. → Sind Sie verheiratet? No do/does helper.
  • 2️⃣W-Wort auf 1, Verb auf 2the question word takes slot 1, the verb slot 2 — Wo wohnen Sie? · Woher kommst du? The Lektion 2 rule, doing a new job.
  • 🧭wo · woher · wohinwhere · where from · where to — her = towards me, hin = away from me. One word, three arrows.
  • 🎁Die Frage schenkt dir das Verbtake the verb from the question and put -e on it — Wo wohnen Sie? → Ich wohne … The single most useful survival trick above your level.

Nomen dieser Lektion (nouns from this Lektion)

  • 🪪der Familienname / die Familiennamensurname, family name
  • 🗣️die Sprache / die Sprachenlanguage
  • 🎨das Hobby / die Hobbyshobby
  • 👶das Kind / die Kinderchild
  • 🔤das Verb / die Verbenverb
  • ❓die Frage / die Fragenquestion
  • 📝das Wort / die Wörterword

Dialoge (dialogues)

Dialog 1 · Im Sprachkurs (in the language class · Sie)
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Guten Morgen! Wie heißen Sie?Good morning! What is your name?
🧑🏽 Herr Khan
Ich heiße Imran Khan.My name is Imran Khan.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin

Ich komme aus Pakistan.I come from Pakistan.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Und wo wohnen Sie jetzt?And where do you live now?

Ich wohne in Berlin.I live in Berlin.

Welche Sprachen sprechen Sie?Which languages do you speak?
🧑🏽 Herr Khan
Ich spreche Urdu, Englisch und etwas Deutsch.I speak Urdu, English and a bit of German.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Sehr gut! Danke schön.Very good! Thank you kindly.

Every question has the verb in -en because it is Sie, and every answer flips it to -e. Herr Khan, surname only (Lektion 1), and etwas Deutsch (Lektion 2) is the honest answer at this level.

Dialog 2 · Auf der Party (at a party · du)
👩 Lena
Hallo! Wie heißt du?Hi! What's your name?
🧑 Bilal
Ich heiße Bilal. Und du?I'm Bilal. And you?
👩 Lena
Ich bin Lena. Woher kommst du?I'm Lena. Where are you from?
🧑 Bilal
Ich komme aus Pakistan. Und du?I'm from Pakistan. And you?
👩 Lena
Aus Österreich. Wie alt bist du?From Austria. How old are you?
🧑 Bilal
Ich bin einundzwanzig. Und du?I'm twenty-one. And you?
👩 Lena
Ich bin neunzehn.I'm nineteen.
🧑 Bilal
Welche Sprachen sprichst du?Which languages do you speak?
👩 Lena
Deutsch und Englisch.German and English.

The du verb forms here are heißt, kommst, sprichst, and bist for sein. Most carry -st; heißt adds only -t because its stem ends in ß. Note sprichst, not sprechst: the vowel changed. And Und du? thrown back after each answer is what keeps a conversation alive.

Dialog 3 · Ja oder Nein (yes or no · Sie)
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Sind Sie verheiratet?Are you married?
👩 Frau Ott
Nein, ich bin nicht verheiratet. Ich bin ledig.No, I am not married. I am single.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Haben Sie Kinder?Do you have children?
👩 Frau Ott
Nein, ich habe keine Kinder.No, I have no children.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Was machen Sie beruflich?What do you do for a living?
👩 Frau Ott
Ich bin Lehrerin.I am a teacher.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Danke. Und wie ist Ihr Familienname?Thanks. And what is your surname?
👩 Frau Ott
Ott. O – Doppel-T.Ott. O – double T.
🧑‍💼 Beamtin
Danke schön!Thank you kindly!

The first two questions start with the VERB, because they are yes/no questions. The last two start with a W-word. Both keep the verb inside the first two slots. And O – Doppel-T is Lektion 5 doing its job.

Dialog 4 · Beide Formen (both forms, back to back)
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Bilal, fragen Sie Lena — formell.Bilal, ask Lena — formally.
🧑 Bilal
Wo wohnen Sie?Where do you live?
👩 Lena
Ich wohne in Wien.I live in Vienna.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Und jetzt informell.And now informally.
🧑 Bilal
Wo wohnst du?Where do you live?
👩 Lena
Ich wohne in Wien.I live in Vienna.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Genau — die Antwort bleibt gleich!Exactly — the answer stays the same!

The point of the whole Lektion in one line: the question changes, the answer does not. Whether you were asked with Sie or du, you answer with ich, and ich has only one form.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · W-Frage, Sie: W-Wort + Verb(-en) + Sie (W-question, formal: question word + verb + Sie)
WoW-Wort · question wordwohnenVerb · -en, position 2Sie?Subjekt · formal you

Wo wohnen Sie? (Where do you live?) The W-word takes slot 1, so the Sie-verb — which keeps the plain dictionary ending -en — sits in slot 2, right where Lektion 2's rule put it.

2 · W-Frage, du: W-Wort + Verb(-st) + du (W-question, informal: question word + verb + du)
WoherW-Wort · question wordkommstVerb · -st, position 2du?Subjekt · informal you

Woher kommst du? (Where do you come from?) Same skeleton as Block 1 — only the verb ending changes, -en → -st, because the subject changed from Sie to du.

3 · Ja/Nein-Frage: Verb + Subjekt + …? (yes/no question: verb + subject)
SindVerb · position 1SieSubjekt · subjectverheiratet?Rest · adjective, end

Sind Sie verheiratet? (Are you married?) No W-word means the verb itself jumps to position 1; there is no do/does helper to reach for. Sie sind verheiratet. → Sind Sie verheiratet?

4 · Die Antwort: Subjekt + Verb(-e) + Rest (the answer: subject + verb + the rest)
IchSubjekt · subjectwohneVerb · -e, position 2in Berlin.Rest · place

Ich wohne in Berlin. Take whichever verb the question handed you — wohnen or wohnst — strip the ending, add -e. It does not matter whether you were asked with Sie or du: the answer always uses ich, and ich has only one ending.

5 · Stammvokal wechselt: sprechen → du sprichst (stem vowel change: to speak → you speak)
SprichstVerb · e → i, position 1duSubjekt · informal youDeutsch?Objekt · language

Sprichst du Deutsch? A handful of verbs swap their vowel for du: sprechen → sprichst, essen → isst, sehen → siehst, geben → gibst. With Sie, these verbs retain their stem: Sprechen Sie Deutsch?

6 · sein und haben: die Rebellen (to be and to have: the rebels)
BistVerb · irregularduSubjekt · informal youverheiratet?Rest · adjective

bin, bist, sind and habe, hast, haben do not follow the regular -en/-st pattern cleanly. The du forms here still end in -st: Bist du verheiratet? Hast du Kinder? (By contrast, du heißt adds only -t after ß.) Sie uses sind with sein and the infinitive-shaped haben: Sind Sie verheiratet? Haben Sie Kinder?

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Die Sie-Form ist faul (the Sie form is lazy): most verbs with Sie use the dictionary form unchanged — kommen, wohnen, heißen. The exception here is sein → Sie sind.
  • du trägst einen Stock: -st (you carry a stick: -st): regular du forms usually carry -st: kommst, wohnst, machst. bist, hast, kannst (are, have, can: du forms): these irregular forms also end in -st.
  • sprechen → sprichst (to speak → you speak): the e shrinks to an i when du is watching. Same for essen → isst, sehen → siehst. heißt, nicht heißst (you are called: heißt, not heißst): the ß already hisses, so the du form adds only -t.
  • wo · woher · wohin (where · where from · where to): her = towards me, hin = away. Where, where-from, where-to — one word, three arrows.
  • Verb nach vorn = Ja/Nein (verb first = yes/no): push the verb to the front and you have asked a yes/no question. Pull it back to slot 2 and it is a statement again.
  • Kein „do" im Deutschen (no "do" in German): German never borrows a helper verb. Reaching for do means you are speaking English with German words.
  • Die Frage schenkt dir das Verb (the question gives you the verb): whatever verb they ask you with, take the stem of its infinitive, put -e on it, and you have your answer — Sprichst du …? → Ich spreche … Only ich bin, weiß, kann, muss, will, mag break the pattern. See the figure above.
  • Ihr und Sie tragen Hüte (Ihr and Sie wear hats): the polite forms wear a capital like a hat. Small sie and ihr mean she/they and her/their — Lektion 24 has the full possessive table.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Wie du heißt? → Wie heißt du? — the verb must sit in position 2, right after the W-word.
  • Du sprechst Deutsch? → Du sprichst Deutsch? — sprechen changes e → i in the du form.
  • Wie heißst du? → Wie heißt du? — the stem already ends in ß, so only -t is added.
  • Sie kommst aus Pakistan? → Kommen Sie aus Pakistan? — Sie takes -en, and a yes/no question puts the verb first.
  • Tun Sie Deutsch sprechen? → Sprechen Sie Deutsch? — German has no do / does helper.
  • (to a stranger) Wie ist dein Familienname? → Wie ist Ihr Familienname? — strangers get Sie and Ihr.
  • Was sind Ihr Hobbys? → Was sind Ihre Hobbys? — plural → -e, like meine and keine.
  • Wie alt sind sie? → Wie alt sind Sie? — polite Sie and Ihr always take a capital.
  • Sind Sie Verheiratet? → Sind Sie verheiratet? — verheiratet is an adjective, small letter.
  • Woher wohnst du? → Wo wohnst du? — woher = where FROM; living happens IN a place.

Dialog Im Bus (On the bus)

  • MaxHallo! Ich bin Max. Wie heißt du?Hi! I'm Max. What's your name?
  • SaraIch heiße Sara. Woher kommst du, Max?My name is Sara. Where do you come from, Max?
  • MaxIch komme aus Österreich. Und du?I come from Austria. And you?
  • SaraAus Pakistan. Ich wohne jetzt in Wien.From Pakistan. I live in Vienna now.
  • MaxWelche Sprachen sprichst du?Which languages do you speak?
  • SaraUrdu, Englisch und etwas Deutsch.Urdu, English and a bit of German.
  • MaxWas machst du beruflich?What do you do for a living?
  • SaraIch bin Studentin. Und du?I am a student. And you?
  • MaxIch bin Lehrer. Bist du verheiratet?I am a teacher. Are you married?
  • SaraNein, ich bin ledig.No, I am single.

Richtig oder falsch? (true or false?)

  1. Max kommt aus Österreich. Max comes from Austria.
  2. Sara wohnt in Berlin. Sara lives in Berlin.
  3. Sara ist verheiratet. Sara is married.

Schreib das fehlende Wort (type it — capital letters count)

  1. Complete the du-form of sprechen (watch the vowel).
    Welche Sprachen du?
  2. Complete the question word meaning "where from".
    kommst du, Max?
  3. Complete the du-form of sein in this yes/no question.
    du verheiratet?
8

Wie geht's? (How are you?)

The most-asked question in German, and the one beginners answer wrongly most often — because the obvious translation, Ich bin gut, means something else entirely.

Die zwei Regeln (the two that carry this Lektion)

1 · Warum mir und nicht ich? (why "mir" and not "ich"?)

German does not say “I am fine”. It says Mir geht es gut — literally “to me it goes well”. es (life, the day, things in general) is the subject; mir says who it is happening to. Urdu says it exactly the same way — میرا حال اچھا ہے — so think in Urdu here, not English. The three forms: mir (I), dir (du), Ihnen (Sie). And Ich bin gut is not “I'm fine” — it means I am skilled.

2 · Ich bin … oder Mir geht es …? (Ich bin … or Mir geht es …?)

Ich bin for a property of you: Ich bin müde, Ich bin krank. Mir geht es for how things are going: Mir geht es gut / schlecht. The test — could you point at yourself and say “I am this”? Tired, yes. Fine, no. And whichever answer you pick, always throw the question back: Und Ihnen? / Und dir? — the echo copies the word the question was built on.

Wortschatz: Frage & Rückfrage (vocabulary: asking & asking back)

Frage (asking)

  • 🎩Wie geht es Ihnen?How are you? (Sie) vee gayt es EE-nn · · formell — always safe with a Sie-person, and the right choice at a first meeting.
  • 👋Wie geht es dir?How are you? (du) vee gayt es DEE-uh · · informell — du becomes dir in the to-you form.
  • 💬Wie geht's?How's it going? vee GAYTS · · neutral — just Wie geht es contracted; the apostrophe is a missing e, like English how's.

Rückfrage (asking back)

  • 🔁Und Ihnen?And you? (Sie) unt EE-nn · · formell — NOT Und Sie? The echo copies the word the question was built on.
  • ↩️Und dir?And you? (du) unt DEE-uh · · informell — giving the question back is not optional; stopping sounds cold.
  • 💐Gute Besserung!Get well soon! GOO-tuh BES-uh-rung · · neutral — the fixed thing you say to someone ill. Gute with -e because die Besserung — like Gute Nacht (Lektion 1).

Wortschatz: Antwort & Ich bin … (vocabulary: answering & the body-state pattern)

Antwort (good to excellent)

  • 🙂Mir geht es gut!I'm fine! mee-uh gayt es GOOT · · neutral — literally "to me it goes well". Never Ich bin gut — that means "I am skilled".
  • 😄Mir geht es sehr gut!I'm very well! mee-uh gayt es zay-uh GOOT · · neutral — sehr = very. One rung up the ladder.
  • 👍Gut, danke!Good, thanks! GOOT, DANG-kuh · · neutral — the short everyday answer. Follow it immediately with Und Ihnen? or Und dir?
  • 🔄Auch gut, danke!Also good, thanks! owkh GOOT, DANG-kuh · · neutral — what you say when they answered first. auch = also.
  • 😐Es geht.So-so. / Not too bad. es GAYT · · neutral — the honest middle. Drop the gut and you are left with just "it goes" — that neutrality IS the meaning.
  • 🌟Ausgezeichnet!Excellent! OWS-guh-ts-EYE-khnet · · neutral — top of the ladder. Long word — break it as OWS-guh-ts-EYE-khnet.
  • ✨Wunderbar!Wonderful! VUN-duh-bar · · neutral — w says v, and the final -bar is BAR with a darkened r.
  • 🤩Fantastisch!Fantastic! fan-TAS-tish · · neutral — final -sch is one sh sound.
  • 👌Prima!Great! PREE-mah · · informell — note the spelling: prima, not primal.
  • 🔥Toll!Awesome! TOL · · informell — short and very common between friends.
  • 💯Super!Super! ZOO-puh · · informell — s before a vowel buzzes: ZOO-puh, not SOO-per.

Ich bin … (body — a property of your body)

  • 😴Ich bin müde.I am tired. ikh bin MEW-duh · · neutral — Ich bin, NOT Mir geht es — tiredness is a property of you, not how life is going.
  • 🤒Ich bin krank.I am ill. ikh bin KRANK · · neutral — same reason as müde. Could you point at yourself and say "I am this"? Then use Ich bin.

Antwort (not so good to awful)

  • 🙁Mir geht es nicht gut.I'm not doing well. mee-uh gayt es nikht GOOT · · neutral — nicht negates the adjective gut — Lektion 2's rule.
  • 😞Mir geht es schlecht.I'm doing badly. mee-uh gayt es SHLEKHT · · neutral — schl- at the start is shl-, and the ch here is the soft kh.
  • 😩Miserabel!Miserable! mee-zeh-RAH-bl · · neutral — bottom of the ladder, alongside furchtbar.
  • 😱Furchtbar!Awful! FURKHT-bar · · neutral — the rough kh, then -bar.
mir · dir · Ihnen (the three to-me / to-you forms)
Empfänger (recipient)Form (form)Beispiel (example)
ich (I / me)mirMir geht es gut. (I'm fine.)
du (you, informal)dirWie geht es dir? (How are you?)
Sie (you, formal)IhnenWie geht es Ihnen? (How are you?)

Regel — kompakt (the five memory-rules from the cards)

  • 🔑Warum mir und nicht ich?the state is the subject; you are the address · neutral — Mir geht es gut = "to me it goes well". Urdu says it the same way: میرا حال اچھا ہے.
  • 🔤mir · dir · Ihnenthe three to-me / to-you forms · neutral — you already used mir in Es tut mir leid (Lektion 2). Same word, same job.
  • ⚠️Ich bin gut ≠ I'm fineIch bin gut means "I am skilled" · neutral — say it to a German and they hear you boasting about your football.
  • 🧭Körper → ich bin, Leben → mir geht esmüde/krank take Ich bin; gut/schlecht take Mir geht es · neutral — the test: could you point at yourself and say "I am this"? Tired, yes. Fine, no.
  • 🔁Und Ihnen? oder Und Sie?the echo copies the question's own word · neutral — Wie geht es Ihnen? → Und Ihnen? · Woher kommen Sie? → Und Sie?

Nomen aus dieser Lektion (nouns from this lesson)

  • 🫀der Körper / die Körperbody · from the rule Körper → ich bin (a property of your body takes Ich bin)
  • 🌱das Leben / die Lebenlife · from Leben → mir geht es (how your life or day is going takes Mir geht es)
  • 💐die Besserung / die Besserungenrecovery, getting better · most often seen here in the fixed phrase Gute Besserung!
  • 🧑‍🤝‍🧑der Freund / die Freundefriend · from Dialog 2, Zwei Freunde (two friends)
  • 📅der Tag / die Tageday · from Dialog 1, Schönen Tag noch! (have a nice rest of the day — Lektion 1)

Vier Dialoge: Wie geht's? (four dialogues: how are you?)

Dialog 1 — Im Büro (at the office · Sie)
👩‍💼 Frau Klein
Guten Morgen, Herr Weber! Wie geht es Ihnen?Good morning, Mr Weber! How are you?
🧑‍💼 Herr Weber
Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?Fine, thanks. And you?
👩‍💼 Frau Klein
Auch gut, danke!Also good, thanks!
🧑‍💼 Herr Weber
Schönen Tag noch!Have a nice rest of the day!
👩‍💼 Frau Klein
Danke, gleichfalls!Thanks, same to you!

The four-move block: ask, answer + give it back, answer again. Und Ihnen?, not Und Sie? The closing pair comes from Lektion 1.

Dialog 2 — Zwei Freunde (two friends · du)
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Hallo Max! Wie geht's?Hi Max! How's it going?
🙋‍♂️ Max
Es geht. Ich bin müde.So-so. I'm tired.
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Oh! Warum?Oh! Why?
🙋‍♂️ Max
Keine Ahnung. Und dir?No idea. And you?
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Mir geht es super! Danke!I'm doing great! Thanks!
🙋‍♂️ Max
Schön! Bis später!Nice! See you later!
🙋‍♀️ Lena
Tschüs!Bye!

Three things at once: Es geht as the honest middle; Ich bin müde with bin, because tiredness is a property of Max; and Mir geht es super with mir, because that is how things are going. The switch between the two patterns is the whole Lektion.

Dialog 3 — Nicht so gut (not so good · du)
👩 Sara
Hallo Ali! Wie geht es dir?Hi Ali! How are you?
🧑 Ali
Mir geht es nicht gut. Ich bin krank.I'm not doing well. I'm ill.
👩 Sara
Oh! Das tut mir leid!Oh! I'm sorry to hear that!
🧑 Ali
Danke.Thanks.
👩 Sara
Gute Besserung!Get well soon!
🧑 Ali
Danke schön! Tschüs!Thank you kindly! Bye!

Das tut mir leid is Lektion 2's Es tut mir leid with Das in front — and it carries the same mir. Gute Besserung takes Gute with -e because die Besserung is a die-word, exactly like Gute Nacht.

Dialog 4 — Der ganze Anfang (the whole opening · Sie)
🧑‍💼 Herr Ott
Guten Tag! Ich heiße Ott. Wie heißen Sie?Hello! My name is Ott. What is your name?
👩‍💼 Frau Khan
Ich heiße Ayesha Khan. Freut mich!My name is Ayesha Khan. Pleased to meet you!
🧑‍💼 Herr Ott
Freut mich auch! Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Khan?Likewise! How are you, Ms Khan?
👩‍💼 Frau Khan
Danke, sehr gut. Und Ihnen?Very well, thanks. And you?
🧑‍💼 Herr Ott
Auch gut, danke. Woher kommen Sie?Also good, thanks. Where do you come from?
👩‍💼 Frau Khan
Ich komme aus Pakistan. Und Sie?I come from Pakistan. And you?
🧑‍💼 Herr Ott
Aus Österreich.From Austria.

The two echoes sit in the same dialogue so you can compare them: Und Ihnen? after Wie geht es Ihnen?, but Und Sie? after Woher kommen Sie? The echo always copies the word the question was built on — the single most useful thing in this Lektion.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Mir + geht + es + Adjektiv — das Grundmuster (the basic pattern)
MirDativ · dative: to megehtVerb · verb, position 2esSubjekt · subjectgut.Adjektiv · adjective

es (life, the day, things in general) is the grammatical subject; mir — sitting in position 1 — says who it is happening to. This is exactly the Urdu pattern, میرا حال اچھا ہے: think in Urdu here, not English.

2 · Es geht mir gut (same sentence; verb still in position 2)
EsSubjekt · subjectgehtVerb · verb, position 2mirDativ · dative: to megut.Adjektiv · adjective

Whatever sits in position 1 gets a little emphasis — mir first stresses ME, es first is the neutral, everyday order. Either way geht never leaves position 2.

3 · Ich bin müde (I am tired: a property of you, not mir)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinVerb · verb: ammüde.Adjektiv · adjective

No mir here at all. müde and krank describe your body, so ich is simply the subject — the test is whether you can point at yourself and say "I am this".

4 · Wie geht es Ihnen? (How are you? — W-question with a dative recipient)
WieW-Wort · question wordgehtVerb · verb, position 2esSubjekt · subjectIhnen?Dativ · dative: formal you

The question word takes position 1, geht stays in position 2, es is still the subject, and the person asked about sits at the end — swap in dir for a friend.

5 · Das Echo kopiert das Wort der Frage (the echo copies the question's word)
UndKonjunktion · conjunctionIhnen?echoes Wie geht es Ihnen?
UndKonjunktion · conjunctionSie?echoes Woher kommen Sie?

The two-word echo is expected in a friendly exchange; stopping after your answer can sound cold. It repeats whichever word the question itself was built on: Ihnen answers Ihnen-questions, while plain Sie answers Sie-questions.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Urdu denkt es richtig vor (Urdu already uses the right pattern): Mir geht es gut is literally "it goes to me well" — Urdu expresses the idea in the same basic way, میرا حال اچھا ہے. Life (or es) is doing the going; you are just the address it is going to. Think in Urdu here, not English, and you get it right first time.
  • mir · dir · Ihnen — chant them as one word: you already met mir in Es tut mir leid (Lektion 2) — same word, same job. Learn the trio together: mir, dir, Ihnen.
  • Ich bin gut ≠ I'm fine — a real false friend: say it to a German and they hear you boasting about your football skills, not your mood. The safe phrase is always Mir geht es gut.
  • Körper → Ich bin, Leben → Mir geht es (body → I am; life → things are going for me): tired and ill (müde, krank) live in your body, so they take Ich bin. Fine and bad (gut, schlecht) describe how your life or day is going, so they take Mir geht es. The test: could you point at yourself and say "I am this"?
  • Es geht (so-so — the motor is running): no gut, no schlecht, just movement. In reply to Wie geht's?, that lack of a positive or negative qualifier makes it a normal, neutral middle answer.
  • Wie geht's = Wie geht es (How's it going? — full form): the apostrophe marks a missing e, exactly like English how's for how is.
  • Der Ball muss zurück (the ball must go back): the question is a ball — answer, then throw Und Ihnen? / Und dir? back, or the conversation stops. And the echo always copies the question's own word: Wie geht es Ihnen? → Und Ihnen?, but Woher kommen Sie? → Und Sie?
  • Gute Besserung, Gute Nacht (get well soon; good night): both take Gute with an -e because die Besserung and die Nacht are both die-words — the Lektion 1 rule, still paying off here.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Ich bin gut. → Mir geht es gut. — Ich bin gut = I am skilled. Fineness is not something you are.
  • Ich geht es gut. → Mir geht es gut. — it is the to-me form: mir, not ich.
  • Wie geht es du? → Wie geht es dir? — du becomes dir in the to-you form.
  • Wie geht es Sie? → Wie geht es Ihnen? — Sie becomes Ihnen.
  • (after Wie geht es Ihnen?) Und Sie? → Und Ihnen? — the echo copies the word the question was built on.
  • Mir bin müde. → Ich bin müde. — tiredness is a property of you → Ich bin.
  • Mir geht es müde. → Ich bin müde. — pick one pattern, not both.
  • Wie geht es Ihnen? — Gut. (and stop) → Gut. Und Ihnen? — not giving the question back sounds cold.
  • Gut Besserung! → Gute Besserung! — die Besserung → -e, exactly like Gute Nacht.
  • primal! → prima! — the word is prima. primal is not German.

Dialog Ayesha ist krank (Ayesha is ill)

  • LenaHallo, Ayesha! Wie geht es dir?Hi, Ayesha! How are you?
  • AyeshaMir geht es nicht gut. Ich bin krank.I'm not doing well. I'm ill.
  • LenaOh, das tut mir leid!Oh, I'm sorry to hear that!
  • AyeshaDanke. Und dir? Wie geht's?Thanks. And you? How's it going?
  • LenaMir geht es super! Danke!I'm doing great! Thanks!
  • AyeshaSchön! Ich bin sehr müde. Bis morgen!Nice! I'm very tired. See you tomorrow!
  • LenaGute Besserung, Ayesha! Tschüs!Get well soon, Ayesha! Bye!
  • AyeshaDanke schön! Tschüs!Thank you kindly! Bye!

Richtig oder falsch? (true or false?)

  1. Ayesha ist krank. Ayesha is ill.
  2. Ayesha sagt: „Mir geht es gut.“ Ayesha says: "I'm fine."
  3. Lena sagt: „Gute Besserung!“ Lena says: "Get well soon!"

Schreib das fehlende Wort (type it — capital letters count)

  1. Complete Lena's informal question (to-you form).
    Wie geht es ?
  2. Complete the to-me form at the start of Ayesha's answer.
    geht es nicht gut.
  3. Complete the fixed phrase you say to someone who is ill.
    Gute !
9

Satzstruktur (Teil 1) (Sentence Structure (Part 1))

German sentences are strict about one thing above all: the finite verb stays in position 2 in a statement and after a W-word, but it jumps to position 1 in a yes/no question. Master the W-Frage and Ja/Nein-Frage patterns here and German word order stops feeling backwards.

Die Position-2-Regel (why German word order feels backwards — and how to fix it in ten seconds)

Die Verb-Zweit-Regel (Verb-Second Rule)
In a German statement, the verb always sits in position 2 — no matter what fills position 1. It doesn't matter whether position 1 holds the subject (Ich) or a time word (Heute); the verb never moves. Compare Ich bin müde. and Heute bin ich müde. — the verb bin stays glued to position 2 in both.
Wenn nicht das Subjekt zuerst kommt (when the subject doesn't come first — T+V+S+Rest)
If a time expression like heute opens the sentence instead of the subject, the subject doesn't vanish — it simply steps back to position 3, right after the verb. This gives the pattern T + V + S + Rest (Time + Verb + Subject + the rest), as in Heute bin ich in Hyderabad. Unlike the comparable English order in “Today I am …”, German puts the finite verb before the subject after an initial time expression — so watch for it, it's a classic exam trap.
W-Fragen: Fragewort + Verb + Subjekt (W-questions: question word + verb + subject)
For questions starting with a question word (wo, woher, …), the question word takes position 1, the verb jumps straight into position 2, and the subject follows in position 3: Wo wohnen Sie? / Woher kommst du? Never insert the subject between the question word and the verb — that is the single most common mistake at this level, so it is very likely to show up on tomorrow's test.
Ja/Nein-Fragen: Verb + Subjekt (yes/no questions: verb + subject)
For a question that expects Ja or Nein as the answer, there is no question word — so the verb itself jumps into position 1, with the subject right behind it in position 2: Haben Sie Kinder? / Sind Sie verheiratet? Compare this to a W-Frage, where the question word takes position 1 and pushes the verb to position 2 — here the verb itself IS position 1.

Vokabel (vocabulary)

  • 📅heutetoday — a time word, a very common sentence-opener that still leaves the verb glued to position 2. HOY-tuh ·
  • 🤲habento have — irregular: ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat; memorise these three forms separately, they don't follow the regular pattern. HAH-ben ·
  • 🎂der Geburtstag / die Geburtstagebirthday — pairs with haben, not sein: Ich habe Geburtstag = "it's my birthday" (literally "I have birthday"). guh-BOORTS-tahk ·
  • 🏠wohnento live / reside — regular: ich wohne, du wohnst, Sie/sie wohnen; needs "in" before a place name. VOH-nen ·
  • 🏷️heißento be called / named — the standard pattern for giving a name is Ich heiße Priyanka. The alternative Ich bin Priyanka. is also grammatical (“I am Priyanka”), but it uses a different construction. HYE-sen ·
  • 🚶kommento come — du kommst; used in Woher kommst du? to ask about origin. KOM-en ·
  • 📍wowhere — asks about a location: where someone currently is or lives. voh ·
  • 🧭woherwhere from — woher = wo + her; asks about origin, not current location. Don't confuse it with plain wo. voh-HAIR ·
  • 😴müdetired — a predicate adjective: pairs with sein (ich bin müde) and never takes an ending in that position. MUE-duh ·
  • 👶das Kind / die Kinderchild / children — after haben you'll often see it bare, with no article: Kinder haben. dee KIN-duh ·
  • 💍verheiratetmarried — a predicate adjective, just like müde: pairs with sein and never changes its ending (Sie sind verheiratet, ich bin verheiratet). fair-HYE-raht-et ·
  • 🇩🇪DeutschlandGermany — used with aus (from): Ich komme aus Deutschland. DOYTCH-lant ·

Beispiel-Sätze (example sentences)

  • 🙋‍♀️Ich heiße Priyanka.My name is Priyanka. — the basic skeleton: Subjekt (ich) + Verb (heiße) + the rest. This is the S+V+Rest pattern in its simplest form. ich HYE-suh pri-YAN-ka ·
  • 🏠Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas.I live in Mirpurkhas. — same shape as Ich heiße Priyanka.: Subjekt + Verb + Rest. in Mirpurkhas is a prepositional place complement, not an object; the verb stays in position 2. ich VOH-nuh in MEER-poor-khahs ·
  • 📍Heute bin ich in Hyderabad.Today I am in Hyderabad. — the time word Heute takes position 1. The verb bin refuses to move: it stays in position 2, so ich slides to position 3. HOY-tuh bin ich in HYE-duh-rah-baht ·
  • 😴Ich bin müde.I am tired. — Subjekt + Verb (bin) + predicate adjective (müde). No object needed: sein just links subject to a description. ich bin MUE-duh ·
  • 🎂Ich habe heute Geburtstag.Today is my birthday. — all three new words together: Subjekt ich, Verb habe in position 2, then heute and Geburtstag trail after it. ich HAH-buh HOY-tuh guh-BOORTS-tahk ·

W-Frage (question-word questions)

  • 📍Wo wohnen Sie?Where do you live? (formal) — the W-word wo grabs position 1. The verb wohnen jumps immediately after it into position 2. Subjekt Sie comes third. voh VOH-nen zee ·
  • 🧭Woher kommst du?Where are you from? (informal) — same pattern as wo: W-word + Verb (kommst) + Subjekt (du). Never let du sneak in before kommst. voh-HAIR komst doo ·
  • 🙋Wie heißen Sie?What is your name? (formal) — the same W-Frage skeleton as Wo wohnen Sie?: Wie (1) + heißen (2) + Sie (3). vee HYE-sen zee ·
  • 👋Wie geht es Ihnen?How are you? (formal) — another W-Frage: Wie (1) + geht (2) + es Ihnen (rest). A fixed greeting phrase, seen again in a later Lektion. vee gayt es EE-nen ·

Ja/Nein-Frage (yes/no questions)

  • 👶Haben Sie Kinder?Do you have children? (formal) — Ja/Nein-Frage: the verb Haben grabs position 1, Subjekt Sie follows in position 2 — the opposite order from a statement. HAH-ben zee KIN-duh ·
  • 💍Sind Sie verheiratet?Are you married? (formal) — same flip: Sind (verb, position 1) + Sie (subject, position 2). Answer with Ja, ich bin verheiratet or Nein, ich bin nicht verheiratet. zint zee fair-HYE-raht-et ·
  • 🏠Wohnst du in Hyderabad?Do you live in Hyderabad? (informal) — Wohnst (verb, position 1) + du (subject, position 2); the -st ending still shows up even without ich or du leading. vohnst doo in HYE-duh-rah-baht ·
  • 🇩🇪Kommen Sie aus Deutschland?Do you come from Germany? (formal) — Kommen (verb, position 1) + Sie (subject, position 2) + aus + place. KOM-en zee ows DOYTCH-lant ·

Kennenlernen (getting to know each other)

Two classmates meet before school.
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Hallo! Ich heiße Ayesha.Hi! My name is Ayesha.
🎒 Sana
Hallo, Ayesha! Ich heiße Sana.Hi, Ayesha! My name is Sana.
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Woher kommst du?Where are you from?
🎒 Sana
Ich komme aus Mirpurkhas. Und du?I come from Mirpurkhas. And you?
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Ich wohne in Hyderabad.I live in Hyderabad.

Notice heiße, komme, and wohne all keep the S+V+Rest order — ich sits in position 1 because nothing else is competing for that spot.

Der Geburtstag (the birthday)

🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Heute habe ich Geburtstag.Today is my birthday.
🎒 Sana
Ja? Wo bist du heute?Yeah? Where are you today?
🙋‍♀️ Ayesha
Ich bin heute in Hyderabad.I'm in Hyderabad today.
🎒 Sana
Ich bin müde.I'm tired.

Two structures at once: Geburtstag haben for the birthday-person construction (Ich habe Geburtstag, not Ich bin Geburtstag), and the W-Frage pattern wo + verb + subject in Wo bist du heute?

Formell oder informell? (formal or informal address)

👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Wo wohnen Sie?Where do you live? (formal)
👧 Schülerin
Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas.I live in Mirpurkhas.
👩‍🏫 Lehrerin
Und woher kommen Sie?And where are you from? (formal)
👧 Schülerin
Ich komme aus Hyderabad.I come from Hyderabad.

The W-Frage skeleton (W-word + verb + subject) stays identical whether the subject is the formal Sie or the informal du — only the verb ending changes.

Theorie (theory) · Satzbau (sentence structure)

1 · Aussage (statement): Subjekt (subject) + Verb (verb) + Rest (remainder)
IchSubjekt · subjectheißeVerb · position 2Priyanka.Rest · remainder

Ich heiße Priyanka. — the simplest German sentence shape: subject in position 1, verb in position 2, everything else trails after. Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas. follows the same pattern.

2 · sein (to be) + Prädikatsadjektiv (predicate adjective) — kein Objekt (no object)
IchSubjekt · subjectbinVerb · position 2müde.Rest · predicate adjective

Ich bin müde. — sein just links the subject to a description; the adjective (müde, verheiratet) is Rest (remainder), never Objekt (object), and never takes an ending here.

3 · Zeit zuerst (time first): T + V + S + Rest (remainder)
HeuteRest · time, position 1binVerb · position 2ichSubjekt · position 3in Hyderabad.Rest · place

Heute bin ich in Hyderabad. — when a time word grabs position 1, the subject steps back to position 3, while the finite verb stays in position 2.

4 · Geburtstag haben (to have a birthday): haben, nicht sein (have, not be)
IchSubjekt · subjecthabeVerb · position 2heuteRest · timeGeburtstag.Akkusativ · object

Ich habe heute Geburtstag. — when the birthday person is the subject, German uses Geburtstag haben, not Ich bin Geburtstag. Here Geburtstag is the object of haben. The separate sentence Heute ist mein Geburtstag. is also correct: there, mein Geburtstag is linked to heute by sein.

5 · W-Fragen (W-questions): Fragewort (question word) + Verb (verb) + Subjekt (subject)
WoW-Wort · question wordwohnenVerb · position 2Sie?Subjekt · position 3

Wo wohnen Sie? / Woher kommst du? — the question word takes position 1, the verb comes straight after it, and the subject comes next in these simple examples. Never put the subject between the question word and the verb.

6 · Ja/Nein-Fragen (yes/no questions): Verb (verb) + Subjekt (subject)
HabenVerb · position 1SieSubjekt · position 2Kinder?Akkusativ · object

Haben Sie Kinder? / Sind Sie verheiratet? — with no question word before it, the finite verb itself leads. This is the only pattern here where the verb is not in position 2.

green = Subjekt (subject, Nominativ) · white = Verb (verb, position 2) · amber = Objekt (object, Akkusativ) · grey = Rest (the rest: adjective, place, time) · blue = W-Wort (question word)

Mehr dazu (more on this)

  • Verb = Position 2 (in statements): picture the finite verb as having a fixed parking spot — spot #2, whether the subject or a time word pulls into spot #1 first. Compare S+V+Rest with T+V+S+Rest: when heute cuts in line, it's the subject that gets bumped to seat #3. In a Ja/Nein-Frage, however, the verb leads in spot #1.
  • Heute bin ich… (Today I am…): heute grabs the front seat, so ich has to slide to the back seat (position 3) — the verb stays in the driver's seat (position 2) the whole time.
  • Wo wohnen Sie? (Where do you live? — formal): the W-word opens the door and the verb walks straight through right behind it — the subject has to wait outside until the verb has entered.
  • woher = wo + her (where from): picture someone pointing back over their shoulder to where they came FROM, not to where they're standing now — don't confuse it with plain wo (where).
  • Ich habe Geburtstag (It's my birthday): when the birthday person is the subject, German uses haben: Ich habe Geburtstag, not Ich bin Geburtstag. The separate sentence Heute ist mein Geburtstag (“Today is my birthday”) is also correct.
  • müde (tired) sounds like “moody”: being tired often makes you moody too — a handy, if approximate, way to remember it.
  • heißen / wohnen / kommen (be called / live / come) — same order every time: three parts of your intro, always ich + verb + info: heiße (your name), wohne (your address), komme (your hometown).
  • Ja/Nein-Frage = Verb zuerst (yes/no question = verb first): no question word to lean on, so the verb steps up and leads — like English “Do you…?”, minus the “do”.

Korrekturen (corrections)

  • Heute ich bin müde. → Heute bin ich müde. — the verb must stay in position 2, right after whatever leads the sentence. The subject can't sneak in before it just because it's the subject.
  • Wo Sie wohnen? → Wo wohnen Sie? — after a W-word the verb comes immediately — the subject goes after the verb, never before it.
  • Ich bin Geburtstag heute. → Ich habe heute Geburtstag. — "Geburtstag haben" uses haben, not sein — you don't "be" a birthday in German, you "have" one.
  • Ich bin müden. → Ich bin müde. — predicate adjectives after sein never take an ending — müde stays müde no matter who is tired.
  • Woher du kommst? → Woher kommst du? — same V2 rule as every W-Frage: the verb jumps to position 2 right after the question word, before the subject.
  • Ich wohne Mirpurkhas. → Ich wohne in Mirpurkhas. — wohnen needs the preposition in before a place name — it can't be dropped.
  • Bin ich heute müde. → Ich bin heute müde. — putting the verb first turns a statement into a question in German. Keep the subject in position 1 unless another element (like heute) replaces it.
  • Heute Geburtstag ich habe. → Heute habe ich Geburtstag. — only one item can occupy position 1. Heute leads, the verb comes right after it, and the subject follows — everything else trails at the end.
  • Sie haben Kinder? → Haben Sie Kinder? — a standard neutral Ja/Nein-Frage puts the verb in position 1, not the subject; subject-first order is limited to a marked confirmation or echo question.

Dialog Heute ist Geburtstag (Today is a birthday)

  • SanaHallo, Bilal! Wo bist du heute?Hi, Bilal! Where are you today?
  • BilalIch bin heute in Hyderabad.I'm in Hyderabad today.
  • SanaAh! Und ich habe heute Geburtstag!Ah! And today is my birthday!
  • BilalJa? Wie alt bist du?Really? How old are you?
  • SanaIch bin zwanzig Jahre alt.I am twenty years old.
  • BilalToll! Bist du müde?Awesome! Are you tired?
  • SanaNein, heute bin ich nicht müde.No, today I'm not tired.
  • BilalKommst du morgen?Are you coming tomorrow?
  • SanaJa, kein Problem. Bis morgen!Yes, no problem. See you tomorrow!
  • BilalBis morgen, Sana!See you tomorrow, Sana!

Richtig oder falsch? (true or false?)

  1. Sana hat heute Geburtstag. Today is Sana's birthday.
  2. Bilal ist heute in Hyderabad. Bilal is in Hyderabad today.
  3. Sana ist müde. Sana is tired.

Schreib das fehlende Wort (type it — capital letters count)

  1. Put the verb in position 2 after "Heute".
    Heute ich nicht müde.
  2. Complete the birthday phrase (haben, not sein).
    Ich heute Geburtstag.
  3. Complete the question word meaning "where".
    bist du heute?

Häufige Ausdrücke, Zahlen & Fragen (common phrases, numbers 0–20 & yes/no questions)

Numbers, everyday rescue phrases, and the moment German flips its word order for yes/no questions — verb first. This is dense, testable material: know du vs. Sie cold, and know that a question starting with a verb is asking for ja or nein.

Die Regel (the rule)

the five things this Lektion turns on

1 · Sie oder du? (formal vs. informal "you")

German splits 'you' into two words depending on who you're talking to. Talk to a teacher, a stranger, or any adult you don't know well, and you use Sie (always capitalized) — Wo wohnen Sie? Talk to a friend, a classmate, or family, and you use du — Woher kommst du? Mixing these up isn't just a grammar slip, it can sound rude.

2 · Personal pronouns replace nouns

Instead of repeating a name or noun every time, German — like English — swaps it for a pronoun. ich (I) and wir (we) cover the first person: Ich wohne in Mirpur-khas means 'I live...' without repeating your name every sentence. The dedicated pronoun list in this lesson introduces only 1st and 2nd person (ich/wir, du/Sie); the full conjugation cards below also show the 3rd-person forms er/sie/es.

3 · Satzstruktur Teil 2: V-S-O für Ja/Nein-Fragen (sentence structure part 2: V-S-O for yes/no questions)

Prüfungstipp: When German asks a question that can be answered with ja or nein, the verb jumps all the way to the front, before the subject: Verb + Subjekt + Objekt. Spielen Sie Fußball? — Spielen (verb) leads, Sie (subject) follows, Fußball (object) closes. Compare this to a statement like Ich heiße Priyanka, which keeps the normal Subjekt + Verb order. If a test question starts with the verb, it's this pattern.

4 · Numbers 0–20: the -zehn pattern (and its one rebel)

From 13 to 19, German numbers are built by taking the digit and adding -zehn (meaning 'ten'): drei + zehn = dreizehn (13), vier + zehn = vierzehn (14). Two digits lose a letter for smoother pronunciation: sechzehn (not sechszehn) and siebzehn (not siebenzehn). zwanzig (20) refuses to follow the pattern at all — it's simply its own word.

5 · Regelmäßige Verben: Das -en-Muster (regular verbs: the -en pattern)

Verbs like wohnen, machen, spielen, and studieren all conjugate exactly the same way in the present tense: drop the -en from the infinitive to find the stem, then add -e (ich), -st (du), -t (er/sie/es and ihr), or -en (wir, Sie, sie). Learn the present-tense pattern once with wohnen and you already know all four.

Wortschatz: Pronomen (vocabulary: pronouns)

  • 🙋ichI ikh · — 1st person singular — pairs with wohne, heiße, verstehe, weiß.
  • 👥wirwe veer · — 1st person plural — 'Wir wohnen in Mirpur' instead of naming everyone in the group.
  • 👉duyou (informal, singular) doo · — Use with friends, classmates, siblings — never with a teacher or a stranger.
  • 🤝Sieyou (formal) zee · — Always capitalized, even mid-sentence — that capital S is the only thing distinguishing it in writing from 'sie' (she/they).

Wortschatz: Fragen (vocabulary: yes/no questions — the V-S-O shape)

  • ⚽Spielen Sie Fußball?Do you play football? SHPEE-len zee FOOS-bal · — Verb jumps to position 1, Sie (subject) comes second, Fußball (object) last — the V-S-O question shape.
  • 🗣️Sprechen Sie Italienisch?Do you speak Italian? SHPREKH-en zee ee-tal-YAY-nish · — Same V-S-O skeleton as Spielen Sie...? — just swap the verb, keep the order.
  • 👂Verstehen Sie mich?Do you understand me? fer-SHTAY-en zee mikh · — If the answer is no, you already know the reply: 'Nein, ich verstehe nicht.'
  • ⏰Haben Sie Zeit?Do you have time? HAH-ben zee tsait · — haben (to have) is irregular here: Sie haben, not 'Sie habt' or 'Sie habe'.
  • 🎂Sind Sie 30 Jahre alt?Are you 30 years old? zint zee DRAI-sig YAH-ruh alt · — sein (to be) is also irregular: sind, not 'seid' or 'bin', because the subject here is Sie.

Wortschatz: Ausdrücke (vocabulary: everyday rescue phrases)

  • 🤷Ich verstehe nichtI don't understand ikh fer-SHTAY-uh nikht · — Your best classroom rescue phrase — say this instead of going quiet when you're lost.
  • 🤔Ich weiß nichtI don't know ikh vais nikht · — Different job from 'ich verstehe nicht': this is about not knowing a fact/answer, not about failing to understand the language.
  • 🙅Keine AhnungNo idea KAI-nuh AH-nung · — A casual shrug of a phrase — fine with friends, a bit too relaxed for a teacher.
  • 👍Kein ProblemNo problem kain pro-BLAYM · — Almost identical to English — one of the easiest phrases in the whole course to remember.
  • ⏳Einen Moment, bitteJust a moment, please AI-nen mo-MENT, BIT-uh · — Buys you thinking time — use it while you search for the word you actually need.
  • ☑️Ja / Nein / VielleichtYes / No / Maybe yah / nain / fee-LAIKHT · — The three answers every V-S-O yes/no question is fishing for.

  • 🔟elf, zwölf, dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn11–15 elf, tsverlf, DRAI-tsayn, FEER-tsayn, FEWNF-tsayn · /ɛlf, t͡svœlf, ˈdraɪ̯ˌt͡seːn, ˈfiːɐ̯ˌt͡seːn, ˈfʏnfˌt͡seːn/ — From 13 onward it's just digit + -zehn (zehn = ten): drei+zehn = dreizehn (13).
  • 2️⃣0️⃣sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn, zwanzig16–20 ZEX-tsayn, ZEEP-tsayn, AKHT-tsayn, NOYN-tsayn, TSVAN-tsig · /ˈzɛçˌt͡seːn, ˈziːpˌt͡seːn, ˈaxˌt͡seːn, ˈnɔɪ̯nˌt͡seːn, ˈt͡svant͡sɪç/ — sechs and sieben each drop a letter here (sechzehn, siebzehn), and zwanzig (20) abandons the -zehn pattern entirely.

Aussage vs. Frage: ein Beispielsatz (statement vs. question: one example sentence)

  • 🙋‍♀️Ich heiße Priyanka.My name is Priyanka. ikh HAI-suh pri-YAN-ka · — A statement, not a question — Subjekt (Ich) first, Verb second. Compare the word order to the questions above.

Compare its Subjekt+Verb order to every Sie-question above — same building blocks, different order.

Konjugation: neun Verben im Präsens (conjugation: nine verbs in the present tense, with the same endings here)

  • 🚏er/sie/es kommthe/she/it comes air/zee/es KOMT ·
  • 🚏wir kommenwe come veer KOM-en ·
  • 🚏ihr kommtyou all come (informal) eer KOMT ·
  • 🚏sie/Sie kommenthey come / you come (formal) zee KOM-en ·

hören (to hear)

  • 👂ich höreI hear ich HUH-ruh ·
  • 👂du hörstyou hear (informal) doo HUHRST ·
  • 👂er/sie/es hörthe/she/it hears air/zee/es HUHRT ·
  • 👂wir hörenwe hear veer HUH-ren ·
  • 👂ihr hörtyou all hear (informal) eer HUHRT ·
  • 👂sie/Sie hörenthey hear / you hear (formal) zee HUH-ren ·

lernen (to learn)

  • ✏️ich lerneI learn ich LEHR-nuh ·
  • ✏️du lernstyou learn (informal) doo LEHRNST ·
  • ✏️er/sie/es lernthe/she/it learns air/zee/es LEHRNT ·
  • ✏️wir lernenwe learn veer LEHR-nen ·
  • ✏️ihr lerntyou all learn (informal) eer LEHRNT ·
  • ✏️sie/Sie lernenthey learn / you learn (formal) zee LEHR-nen ·

sagen (to say)

  • 💬ich sageI say ich ZAH-guh ·

  • 🚶er/sie/es gehthe/she/it goes air/zee/es GAYT · — The -t ending — ihr also takes this exact ending. This is the form behind 'Wie geht's?' and 'Es geht.'
  • 🚶wir gehenwe go veer GAY-en ·
